title: How much does it really cost to import a car from the USA?
metaTitle: How much does it cost to import a car from the USA? | Carglo
description: Import a car from the USA to Europe: real cost breakdown of auction fees, transport, freight, customs duty, VAT, port fees and registration – with an example.
lead: The price on Copart or IAAI is only the beginning. By the time the car stands registered in front of your house, you usually pay 1.6 to 2 times the hammer price. Here is where that money goes – line by line, with a worked example for a $10,000 car and tips on how to keep the total down.

blocks.p: For a typical passenger car bought for $10,000 at a US auction, expect a total of roughly $16,000–19,000 delivered to your door in the EU, before national registration costs. The biggest items after the car itself are import VAT, customs duty and transport. Repairs of damaged cars come on top, and for non-running salvage cars they can be the largest single item.

The cost of importing a car from the USA to Europe falls into three groups: costs in the US (auction, broker, inland truck), the crossing (ocean freight and insurance) and costs in the EU (duty, VAT, port, delivery and registration). The first two groups are paid in dollars, the last one in euros or your local currency.

blocks.h2: 1. The purchase: bid plus auction fees

blocks.p: Copart and IAAI charge a buyer fee that grows with the price, plus fixed internet-bidding, gate and environmental fees. Clean-title and salvage-title cars have different fee schedules. If you bid through a broker, add the broker’s commission.

ul: Buyer fee: tiered by price, often $600–1,000 on a $10,000 car
Virtual/internet bid fee and gate fee: about $100–200
Broker commission: typically $200–500 per car
Storage: charged per day if you pay or collect late

blocks.h2: 2. Getting the car to the port

blocks.p: A truck takes the car from the auction yard to the export port (New Jersey, Savannah, Houston or Los Angeles). Distance matters: a yard close to the port costs a few hundred dollars, a cross-country haul over $1,000. A non-running car needs a forklift and winch, which adds a surcharge. Cars from the West Coast either cross the country by truck or sail a much longer route through the Panama Canal.

A shared container (usually 3–4 cars) is the cheapest safe option: about $1,000–1,600 per car from the East Coast to North Sea ports. RoRo is cheaper for running cars but less protected. Marine insurance costs about 1.5% of the car’s value and is part of the customs value. Sailing from the East Coast to Bremerhaven, Rotterdam or Antwerp takes about two weeks; the whole journey from auction to EU port usually four to eight weeks.

Duty is charged on the customs value – the CIF value: price, auction fees, transport to the EU border and insurance. For passenger cars it is 10% (CN code 8703), for pickups 22%, for motorcycles 6–8%. Cars over 30 years old in original condition can be duty-free as collector’s items. Import duty on cars is the same in every EU country, because the EU is one customs union.

blocks.h2: 5. Import VAT – in the country of clearance

blocks.p: VAT is charged on the customs value plus duty and the transport costs to the first destination in the EU. The rate is the one of the country where the car is cleared – from 17% in Luxembourg to 27% in Hungary. That is why the choice of port can change the total by hundreds of euros. A private buyer cannot reclaim this VAT.

In the EU port you pay terminal handling and container unloading (about €400–500) and a customs agent (about €250). Then the car travels to your address by car carrier or tow truck, priced per kilometre. Finally come national costs: inspection, lighting conversion, translations, registration fees and – in many countries – a registration tax based on CO₂, price or engine size. These national costs differ so much between member states that they must be checked for the country where the car will be registered.

The VAT base here is the CIF value plus duty plus the costs after the border up to the destination (13,030 + 1,303 + 1,250 = 15,583 dollars). The example uses round numbers for orientation. Exchange rates, the clearance country, the car type and your address change the result – the calculator works it out for your specific car and compares all 43 EU ports door to door; you only enter your address.

blocks.tip: Plan a buffer of 10–15% for surprises: storage fees, a delayed vessel, a customs inspection or hidden damage. The calculator shows these risks in its pessimistic scenario.

blocks.p: Importing pays off when the same car costs clearly more in your home market after all of the above – typically for well-equipped SUVs, pickups, muscle cars, US-only models and lightly damaged late-model cars that can be repaired cheaply. It rarely pays for cheap mass-market cars, where fixed costs such as freight, port fees and conversion eat the price advantage.

ol: Buy close to an export port to save on inland transport.
Use a shared container instead of an exclusive one.
Compare ports of clearance: lower VAT in another EU country can beat the extra road transport.
Check the auction fee tiers – a few dollars over a threshold can raise the fee.
Pay the auction in USD with a low-margin currency exchange.
Pay and arrange pick-up on time so you never pay storage.

faq.q: Is import VAT refundable for a private buyer?
faq.a: No. A private person pays import VAT as a final cost. A VAT-registered company can usually deduct it, or use customs procedure 4200 when the car goes on to another EU country.

faq.q: Do I pay VAT on the shipping costs too?
faq.a: Yes. The VAT base includes the customs value, the duty and the transport costs to the first destination in the EU.

faq.q: How much does it cost to ship a car from the USA to Europe?
faq.a: In a shared container, about $1,000–1,600 per car from the East Coast to North Sea ports, plus about 1.5% of the value for insurance. RoRo is cheaper but only for running cars.

title: How to buy a car at Copart or IAAI from Europe
metaTitle: How to buy at Copart or IAAI from Europe – step by step | Carglo
description: How to buy at Copart or IAAI from Europe: registering, brokers, deposits, bidding, payment deadlines and storage fees explained step by step.
lead: Copart and IAAI sell hundreds of thousands of cars every month, many of them to buyers in Europe. Here is how bidding from abroad works, how to choose a broker, how to read a listing and which fees and deadlines you must not miss.

blocks.p: Many lots can only be bought with a dealer licence, and some states restrict who may buy salvage vehicles. That is why most European buyers bid through a registered broker (also called an agent or importer) who places the bids on your behalf under their licence. The broker charges a fixed commission per car.

A good broker does more than click the bid button. They check the lot, explain fees, pay the auction, organise the truck to the port, handle the title and export paperwork and book the container. Ask in advance exactly which of these services the commission covers.

ul: Clear price list: commission, document fee, export fee, payment by bank transfer
Access to both Copart and IAAI and to the lots you want (salvage, dealer-only)
Own or partner warehouse at the export port and regular containers to your preferred EU port
Photos of the car at the warehouse before loading
Written agreement and a company you can verify

ol: Choose a broker and sign the agreement; you get access to bidding through their account.
Pay the security deposit – usually about 10% of your maximum bid.
Find the car, read the condition report and check the VIN history.
Set your maximum bid including all fees – not just the hammer price.
Bid in the preliminary round or live; the highest bid wins if it meets the seller’s reserve.
Pay within the deadline (usually 2–3 business days) by bank transfer.
Arrange pick-up quickly – free storage is short, then a daily fee is charged.
The car is transported to the port, and the title goes to the exporter for customs.

ul: Title type: clean, salvage, rebuilt or certificate of destruction / parts only
Primary and secondary damage, airbags, odometer status
Run and Drive / Engine Starts / Enhanced Vehicles labels – verified only at check-in, not guaranteed
Keys present, location of the yard and its distance to the port
Seller type: insurance company, dealer, rental company

blocks.tip: ‘Run and Drive’ means the car started and moved forward at check-in. It does not mean it is roadworthy – plan for a technical check after arrival.

blocks.h2: Copart vs IAAI at a glance

head: Copart
IAAI
rows: Online, preliminary bids then live auction
Online, pre-bid then live auction (some Buy Now)
Insurers, dealers, rental and finance companies
Mostly insurers, also dealers and fleets
Tiered buyer fee plus fixed fees
Tiered buyer fee plus fixed fees

blocks.p: Both auctions work in a similar way, so compare the same car type on both and do not limit yourself to one. Fee schedules change from time to time; always check the current one for the title type and price level you are bidding at.

Besides the buyer fee, auctions add internet-bidding, gate, environmental and title-handling fees. Late payment and late pick-up cost extra, and relisting fees apply if you do not pay. Your broker adds a commission and sometimes a fee for documents and export.

Work backwards: start from what the car may cost at your door – including duty, VAT, transport and registration – and from the value it will have in your market after repairs. The difference is your maximum, and the calculator turns it into a bid in dollars. As a rule of thumb, everything after the hammer price adds 60–100% on a $10,000 car, so a car worth €20,000 at home rarely justifies a bid much above $10,000–11,000.

ul: Bidding emotionally in the live round and going past your maximum
Ignoring the yard location – a car in California costs far more to ship than one in New Jersey
Paying late and losing the deposit or paying storage
Trusting the photos alone on cars with flood or fire damage

faq.q: Can I cancel after winning?
faq.a: Usually not without penalty. If you do not pay, the deposit is forfeited and relisting fees may apply.

faq.q: How long from winning to the car in Europe?
faq.a: Typically 4–8 weeks: payment and pick-up 1–2 weeks, transport to the port and loading 1–3 weeks, sailing 2–5 weeks.

faq.q: Can I register on Copart myself from Europe?
faq.a: You can open a basic account, but many lots require a dealer licence. Most European buyers therefore bid through a broker’s licence.

title: Salvage title cars from the USA: what you need to know
metaTitle: Salvage title cars from the USA – risks and costs | Carglo
description: Salvage title car in Europe: what clean, salvage, rebuilt and parts-only titles mean, whether you can register it in the EU and how to budget repairs.
lead: Most cars on Copart and IAAI have a salvage title – that is why they are so cheap. In the EU the title brand itself does not stop registration, but it says a lot about the risk you are buying. This guide explains the title types, the real risks and how to budget so a bargain does not become a money pit.

ul: Clean – no total loss recorded
Salvage – declared a total loss by an insurer (collision, flood, theft recovery, hail)
Rebuilt / reconstructed – a former salvage car repaired and re-inspected in the US
Certificate of destruction / parts only / non-repairable – meant for parts; avoid if you want to register the car

blocks.p: An insurer declares a total loss when the repair cost exceeds a set share of the car’s value, so a salvage title does not always mean heavy damage. An expensive car with a modest dent, a hail-damaged car or a stolen-and-recovered car can all end up with a salvage brand. The names and thresholds differ by US state.

blocks.h2: Can a salvage car be registered in Europe?

blocks.p: Yes. EU countries do not use US title brands; what matters is that the repaired car passes the technical inspection and meets EU lighting and safety requirements. The salvage history may, however, lower resale value and some insurers ask about it. Some countries also record a previous total loss or require a more detailed inspection of repaired structural parts, so check the rules of the country where you will register.

Photos show the visible damage, not what is behind it: bent frames, deployed airbags and their sensors, electronics after flooding, missing parts. Flood cars are the riskiest – corrosion and electrical faults appear weeks later.

head: Damage type
Risk
What to watch
rows: Paintless dent repair cost, glass, roof
Wiring looms, plastics, structural heat damage

blocks.tip: Budget repairs at 30–40% of the price for cars that do not run, and keep an extra reserve for hidden damage. The calculator proposes these amounts automatically.

ol: Check the VIN history for previous accidents and flood records.
Prefer cars with front or rear damage only, without airbag deployment.
Get a repair estimate from a body shop that knows the model before you bid.
Check parts availability and prices in your country.
Leave room in the budget: the cheapest car is often the most expensive project.

blocks.p: Treat a salvage car as a project, not a finished car. Add the full landed cost (auction fees, transport, freight, duty, VAT, port and delivery), then repairs, the EU lighting conversion, inspection and registration. Compare the result with the price of an equivalent undamaged car in your country, minus a discount for the accident history when you sell. If the margin is thin, a clean-title car or a lighter damage category is usually the better deal.

Remember that US parts for EU-spec equivalents are not always identical: headlights, bumpers with side markers and some electronics differ. Ordering parts from the US adds shipping, duty and VAT, so check prices and delivery times before you bid.

blocks.h2: Salvage vs clean title: quick comparison

head: Salvage
Clean
rows: Lower, history visible in VIN reports
Same rules, on the price paid
Same rules, on the price paid

blocks.h2: What happens at the EU inspection

blocks.p: The inspector does not care about the US title brand, but does look closely at a repaired car: the VIN on the body and on the plate must match the documents, the airbags and seatbelts must work without warning lights, and the lighting, brakes and steering must meet EU standards. Poorly repaired structural parts or a car that pulls to one side can fail. A professional repair with invoices and photos of the work makes the inspection easier and later helps when you sell the car.

A good rule is to send the photos and the VIN to the workshop that will repair the car before you bid. They can tell you which parts are needed, roughly what they cost locally and whether the damage looks structural.

faq.q: Does a salvage title affect customs duty?
faq.a: No. Duty and VAT are based on the price paid and transport costs, whatever the title.

faq.q: Is a rebuilt title better?
faq.a: It shows the car was repaired and inspected in the US, but the quality of that repair varies. Inspect it like any damaged car.

faq.q: Can I register a parts-only or non-repairable car in the EU?
faq.a: In practice, no. Such documents mean the car is meant for parts; avoid these lots if you want to drive the car.

title: Customs duty and VAT on imported cars, explained
metaTitle: Customs duty and import VAT on cars – how it works | Carglo
description: Import duty on cars in the EU explained: customs value (CIF), duty rates 10% / 22%, import VAT, procedure 4200 and a worked example.
lead: Customs is where most first-time importers get their numbers wrong. Two rules explain almost everything: duty is charged on the CIF value, and VAT on top of it in the country of clearance. Below you will find what goes into each base, the current duty rates and a worked example you can repeat for your own car.

blocks.p: The customs value of a car bought outside the EU is its transaction value plus the costs of bringing it to the EU border: auction fees, transport to the export port, ocean freight and insurance. Costs after the border – unloading, transport inside the EU – are not part of it.

ul: Included: price paid, auction and broker fees, inland transport in the exporting country, export handling, ocean freight, marine insurance
Not included: EU port handling after arrival, customs agent, road transport inside the EU, registration costs

blocks.p: If insurance was not bought, customs may add a notional amount. If freight was paid as a lump sum for several cars, it is split per car. Invoices in dollars or yen are converted at the official customs exchange rate valid for the month of the declaration.

The rates are set at EU level and are the same in every member state. Classification matters: a pickup classified as a goods vehicle pays 22%, while the same model classified as a passenger car pays 10%. The collector’s rate requires the vehicle to be at least 30 years old, in original condition without substantial changes to the main components, and of historical interest; some cars also need a separate import VAT treatment, so check with a customs agent.

VAT is calculated on the customs value plus the duty and the transport costs to the first destination in the EU. It is paid in the member state where the car is released for free circulation, at that country’s standard rate. Some countries also charge an excise or registration tax later – these are national and differ a lot.

Standard VAT rates range from 17% in Luxembourg to 27% in Hungary; Germany charges 19%, the Netherlands and Belgium 21%, Poland 23%, Denmark and Sweden 25%. Because you pay the rate of the clearance country, the port you choose has a direct effect on the bill.

In this example taxes add about a third to the CIF value. For a pickup at 22% duty the same car would pay 2,640 in duty and correspondingly more VAT, which is why classification is worth checking before you buy.

ol: The car arrives and is stored in a temporary storage area at the port.
A customs agent files the import declaration with the invoice, fee receipts, freight invoice and bill of lading.
Customs may check the documents or inspect the car.
You pay duty and VAT (often through the agent).
The car is released for free circulation and you receive the customs documents needed for registration.

blocks.p: A VAT-registered company importing a car that goes straight on to another EU country can clear it under procedure 4200: no import VAT is paid in the country of arrival, and the buyer accounts for VAT in its own country under the reverse charge. Private persons cannot use it.

blocks.tip: Keep the purchase invoice, auction fee receipts, freight invoice and bill of lading – customs may challenge the declared value, and these documents prove it.

blocks.h2: Common mistakes with duty and VAT

ul: Calculating VAT only on the car price instead of on CIF + duty + transport to destination
Forgetting that auction and broker fees are part of the customs value
Assuming a pickup pays 10% like a passenger car
Expecting a private buyer to reclaim import VAT
Forgetting national registration or excise taxes that come after customs

blocks.p: The calculator applies these rules automatically and shows duty and VAT for every EU port of clearance, so you can see how the total changes with the clearance country.

faq.q: Can customs raise the value of my car?
faq.a: Yes, if the declared price looks unrealistically low. Proof of the auction result and payments usually settles it.

faq.q: Is duty lower for electric cars?
faq.a: No, battery electric passenger cars also pay 10%. Some countries have lower registration taxes for EVs.

faq.q: Where do I pay VAT if I clear in another EU country?
faq.a: In the country of clearance, at its rate. You then register the car at home with the customs documents; national registration taxes still apply there.

title: Registering an imported car: documents and steps
metaTitle: Registering a car imported from the USA or Japan | Carglo
description: How to register an imported car in the EU: documents, technical inspection, lighting and speedometer changes, approval and registration tax.
lead: Customs clearance is only half of the job. Before the car gets plates, it has to meet EU technical requirements and you need a set of documents – most of them translated. The exact procedure depends on the country of registration, but the steps below are much the same across the EU.

ol: Clear the car through customs and keep the customs declaration showing duty and VAT paid.
Have the necessary technical changes made (lighting, speedometer, rear fog light).
Pass the individual approval or first technical inspection for imported vehicles.
Pay any national registration tax and fees.
Register the car at the national registration authority and get plates.

ul: Title or export certificate and the purchase invoice
Customs declaration showing duty and VAT paid
Bill of lading
Sworn translations of foreign-language documents
Inspection certificate / conformity confirmation
Proof of insurance and identity

blocks.p: The original US title is usually handed over at export or kept by the exporter, so make sure you receive either the original or the document your registration authority accepts instead. Japanese cars come with an export certificate, which needs a translation in most countries.

US cars usually need their lighting adapted: red rear indicators and side markers do not meet EU rules, and headlights may need a different beam pattern. Speedometers must show km/h. A rear fog light is mandatory. Japanese cars are right-hand drive, which most countries accept with adjusted headlights.

A car without an EU type approval goes through an individual approval or a thorough first inspection. The inspector checks identification (VIN), lighting, emissions and safety equipment. Plan this step with a workshop that knows imported cars.

Some countries accept a data sheet from the manufacturer or an independent technical service, others want measurements of noise and emissions. Newer cars sometimes need a manufacturer confirmation of technical data. Ask the inspection station in advance which papers they want – it saves a second visit.

With the inspection certificate you register the car at the national registration authority. Several countries charge a one-off registration tax based on CO₂, price or engine size; others charge only a fee for plates and documents. Some set a deadline after import, often 30 days.

Registration taxes can be the largest cost after VAT in some countries and almost nothing in others, so look them up for your country before you bid. The calculator includes them for the country you register in.

blocks.tip: Ask the workshop for the list of required modifications before you buy – conversions on some models cost far more than on others.

blocks.p: Lighting conversion and inspection take from a few days to a few weeks, depending on parts and the queue at the inspection station. Translations can be ordered as soon as you have scans of the title and invoice, so start early. Overall, plan two to six weeks from customs release to plates.

To move an unregistered car on public roads you usually need temporary or export plates and a short-term insurance policy. Rules for these differ by country: some issue temporary plates only after a valid inspection, others allow a transfer drive to the inspection station. If the car is damaged or not yet converted, transport it on a car carrier instead.

ul: Missing or wrong title: the VIN on the documents must match the car exactly
Translations not done by a sworn translator where the authority requires it
Conversion done without the parts or certificates the inspector expects
Missing proof of customs clearance from the country where the car was released
Deadlines after import missed, leading to fines in some countries

blocks.p: Keep copies of every document and invoice in one folder. If you sell the car later, a complete import file with customs papers, inspection reports and repair invoices adds to its value.

faq.q: Do I need a certificate of conformity (CoC)?
faq.a: Cars built for the US or Japan have no EU CoC. They are registered through individual approval or a national inspection procedure instead.

faq.q: Can I drive the car home from the port?
faq.a: Only on temporary plates with insurance, and only if the car is roadworthy. Otherwise use a car carrier or tow truck.

faq.q: Can I register the car in my country if I cleared it in another EU country?
faq.a: Yes. The customs declaration from any EU country proves the car is in free circulation; you then follow your national registration procedure.

title: Bremerhaven, Rotterdam or Antwerp? How to choose the port of clearance
metaTitle: Which EU port to clear an imported car? Comparison | Carglo
description: Bremerhaven vs Rotterdam vs Antwerp for car import: how the port changes import VAT, fees, sailing time and delivery – and how to find the cheapest of 43 EU ports.
lead: Most cars from the USA land in Bremerhaven, Rotterdam or Antwerp – but they can be cleared in any of 43 EU ports. The port decides the VAT rate, the port fees and how far the car travels by road. Here is how to compare them for your address.

ol: Import VAT: you pay the rate of the port country – 19% in Germany, 21% in the Netherlands and Belgium, up to 25% in Scandinavia.
Fees: terminal handling, devanning and the customs agent differ by port.
Road distance: the cheaper VAT port may be far from your home.

head: Port
Country
Import VAT
Typical sailing from US East Coast
rows: Longer, often via a North Sea hub
Longer, often via a North Sea hub

blocks.p: Bremerhaven is one of Europe’s largest car terminals and has frequent container and RoRo services from the US, which keeps prices competitive. Rotterdam and Antwerp are equally well connected and are often the natural choice for Benelux, France and western Germany. Hamburg is an alternative for northern and eastern Germany, while Gdynia and Klaipėda serve Central and Eastern Europe and the Baltics.

On a VAT base of €15,000, two percentage points of VAT mean €300. Clearing in Germany at 19% instead of a 21% country therefore saves €300 – but only if the extra road transport costs less than that and you still end up with the documents you need for registration at home. For a high-VAT country such as Hungary (27%) or the Nordic countries (25–25.5%), the difference to a 19% port is larger and can easily justify a longer drive.

If your home country has a high VAT rate, clearing in a country with a lower one can save more than the extra road transport costs. Some countries additionally charge excise or registration tax at home, so the comparison must be done door to door.

Unloading a shared container and terminal handling usually cost about €400–500 per car, and a customs agent about €250, with differences between ports. Road transport is priced per kilometre: a car carrier is cheaper per car on popular routes, a tow truck is faster but dearer for long distances. A non-running car limits your options and makes distance more expensive.

From the US East Coast the North Sea ports are the fastest (about 2 weeks). From Japan and the UAE, ships come through Suez, so Mediterranean ports such as Koper, Genoa or Piraeus are a week or more faster than the North Sea.

blocks.h2: How to choose: a quick method

ol: List the 3–6 ports closest to your address by road.
For each, add port fees, customs agent and delivery cost to your door.
Calculate VAT at each port country’s rate on CIF + duty + transport to destination.
Add your national registration costs, which do not depend on the port.
Pick the lowest door-to-door total, then check sailing frequency from your US port.

blocks.tip: Enter your address in the calculator: it prices every EU port door to door and picks the cheapest automatically.

ul: Sailing frequency: a port with weekly departures from your US port gets your car faster
Customs agent: an agent who handles many private imports avoids delays
Storage: free days at the terminal are limited, then daily storage is charged
Pick-up: some terminals release cars only to registered transport companies
Documents: make sure the agent sends the customs papers your registration authority needs

blocks.p: The cheapest port on paper is not always the best if containers to it are rare or the agent is slow. Ask your broker which EU ports they ship to regularly and compare those first. For running cars on RoRo, check which ports the RoRo lines from your US port actually call at.

faq.q: Can I clear the car in another country and register it at home?
faq.a: Yes. You pay import VAT in the port country and register the car at home with the customs documents.

faq.q: Which ports handle the most cars from the USA?
faq.a: Bremerhaven, Rotterdam, Antwerp and Hamburg on the North Sea, plus Baltic ports such as Gdynia and Klaipėda for Central and Eastern Europe.

faq.q: Is Bremerhaven or Rotterdam cheaper?
faq.a: Germany’s 19% VAT is lower than the Netherlands’ 21%, but port fees and road distance to your home decide. Compare both door to door.

title: Importing a JDM car from Japan: auction sheets, grades and costs
metaTitle: Import a JDM car from Japan – auction sheets & costs | Carglo
description: Import a JDM car from Japan to Europe: how USS and TAA auctions work, how to read an auction sheet and grades, right-hand drive rules and total costs.
lead: Japanese auctions are famous for honest grading and cars in excellent condition. With a reliable exporter, buying a JDM car is safer than buying blind from US auctions – if you understand the auction sheet. This guide covers how buying works, how to read grades and what the import costs in the EU.

blocks.p: Auctions such as USS, TAA, CAA and JU are open to licensed dealers. You buy through an exporter: you choose cars, set a maximum bid, and the exporter bids, pays, deregisters the car for export and ships it.

ol: Choose an exporter with experience shipping to the EU and agree the fees in writing.
Pay a deposit and get access to auction listings.
Shortlist cars and ask for translated auction sheets and extra photos.
Set a maximum bid; the exporter bids on your behalf.
Pay the car and fees after the auction, usually within a few days.
The exporter deregisters the car, issues the export certificate and books shipping.
The car sails to the chosen EU port, where it is cleared and delivered.

ul: Overall grade: 6–5 nearly new, 4.5–4 very good, 3.5 average, R/RA repaired accident car
Interior grade: A to D
Body map: A = scratch, U = dent, W = wave/repair, S = rust, C = corrosion, with a number for size
Inspector notes – always get them translated

head: Grade
Meaning
Typical buyer
rows: Buyers who want a showroom car
Average, visible wear or small repairs
Buyers who check what was repaired

blocks.tip: An R or RA grade is not always bad, but ask what was repaired – frame repairs are a different story from a replaced bumper.

blocks.p: Add the exporter’s fee, inland transport in Japan, export documents and freight. Ships go via Suez: about 5–6 weeks to the North Sea, less to Mediterranean ports. Duty is 10% for passenger cars and import VAT is paid in the country of clearance.

Customs value is calculated in the same way as for US cars: price plus fees, inland transport, freight and insurance up to the EU border. On top come import VAT at the clearance country’s rate (e.g. 21%), port and agent fees, delivery and national registration costs. Classic JDM cars over 30 years old in original condition may qualify as collector’s vehicles with 0% duty.

Typical choices are sports and tuner cars from the 1990s and 2000s, kei cars, rare trim levels and Japan-only models of well-known brands. Popular cars attract many bidders, so prices for clean, unmodified examples have risen. Heavily modified cars may be harder to register, because every change must be approved in the inspection.
Most EU countries register RHD cars, usually after headlight adjustment. A few restrict them for permanent registration – check your national rules before buying.

blocks.h2: Japan vs USA: which is safer?

blocks.p: US auctions sell many damaged cars with limited information, while Japanese auctions mostly sell used cars in running condition with an independent inspection sheet. In return, the trip from Japan is longer, the car is right-hand drive and the choice of EU-relevant models is narrower. For enthusiasts looking for a specific model, Japan is often the better source; for cheap late-model cars, the US offers more.

ul: Experience with EU customers and with the port you want to use
Transparent fees: auction fee, exporter commission, inland transport, documents, freight
Full auction sheet with translation and extra photos on request
Container shipping to Europe, not only RoRo
Clear payment terms and a company you can verify

blocks.p: Ask the exporter for a full example invoice of a recent car shipped to Europe. It shows all fees in one place and lets you calculate your own maximum bid in yen before the auction, with the EU duty, VAT and delivery added in the calculator.

faq.q: Are Japanese mileages reliable?
faq.a: Generally yes – auction sheets and export certificates record mileage, and rollbacks are rare compared with other markets.

faq.q: What about rust?
faq.a: Cars from northern Japan (Hokkaido) can have underbody rust from road salt; the sheet marks it as S or C.

faq.q: How long does shipping from Japan to Europe take?
faq.a: About 5–6 weeks to North Sea ports via Suez, less to Mediterranean ports such as Koper, Genoa or Piraeus.

title: 12-point checklist before you bid on a car abroad
metaTitle: Checklist before bidding on a car from the USA or Japan | Carglo
description: Checklist for buying a car at auction in the USA or Japan: 12 checks on VIN history, title, damage, fees, transport, taxes and registration.
lead: An auction gives you minutes to decide. These twelve points take an evening and save you from the most expensive mistakes. Use them for Copart, IAAI or Japanese auctions alike, and go through them for every car on your shortlist before you place a bid.

ol: Run a VIN history report: accidents, flood, mileage, theft.
Check the title type – avoid parts-only and non-repairable certificates.
Study every photo: panel gaps, airbags, water lines, engine bay.
Read the condition labels as information, not a guarantee.
Check the yard location and the distance to the export port.
Calculate all auction and broker fees for your bid level.
Get the full landed cost: freight, duty, VAT, port, delivery.
Compare ports of clearance for your address.
Get a repair estimate and parts prices in your country.
Check what the car must change to be registered (lights, speedometer).
Plan the timing: payment and pick-up deadlines, sailing, inspection.
Set a maximum bid – and stick to it.

blocks.tip: Do steps 6–8 in the calculator: it adds all fees and taxes and shows optimistic, average and pessimistic totals.

blocks.p: Start with the VIN. A Carfax or AutoCheck report shows previous accidents, insurance claims, flood records and odometer readings. Compare the mileage with the photos of the dashboard and the wear of the seats and pedals. Check the title type in the listing and, for salvage cars, whether the damage matches the history.

Then go through the photos slowly: uneven panel gaps point to structural damage, a deployed airbag means expensive repairs, and a line of dirt inside the doors or on the seats is a sign of flood. Look at the engine bay and under the car where possible. Labels such as Run and Drive are recorded at check-in only and are not a guarantee.

head: Cost item
Where to check
Typical share on a $10,000 car
rows: Auction fee table, broker price list
Rate of the clearance country, e.g. 21%

blocks.p: Add repairs, lighting conversion, inspection and national registration costs. Compare the total with the price of the same car in your country. The difference, minus a reserve, is the most you should spend, and that sets your maximum bid.

blocks.h2: Before the auction: logistics and paperwork

ul: Confirm with your broker or exporter which port they ship from and how often
Know the payment deadline and have the money ready in the right currency
Arrange pick-up before free storage runs out
Decide where the car will be cleared and who will be the customs agent
Ask a workshop which conversions and inspections the model needs
Bidding up to the market price without counting fees and taxes
Forgetting storage fees when pick-up is delayed
Underestimating repairs of ‘minor’ front damage
Ignoring the registration tax in the home country
Buying a car that needs parts which are expensive or slow to get in Europe

blocks.p: Place your maximum as a preliminary bid or bid live, but decide the limit beforehand and do not raise it in the heat of the moment. If you lose, there will be another car next week – auctions list thousands every day.

ol: Pay the auction and fees before the deadline.
Confirm the pick-up date with the transport company.
Ask for photos of the car at the export warehouse and check the keys and title are there.
Get the bill of lading and send the documents to your customs agent.
Order translations and book the workshop for conversion and inspection.

blocks.p: Following these steps keeps costs predictable from the auction to registration. Most expensive surprises – storage, demurrage at the port, a second inspection – come from small delays that pile up, not from one big mistake.

faq.q: How much should I keep in reserve?
faq.a: At least 10–15% of the total for surprises, more for non-running cars.

faq.q: Is a VIN report enough?
faq.a: It is essential but not complete – combine it with the photos, the condition report and a repair estimate.

faq.q: What is the most important check before bidding at a US auction?
faq.a: The full landed cost. Most losses come from bidding without counting fees, transport, duty, VAT and registration.
